claims.claim: Howell, running for the open Seat D, agreed with the idea of a data center moratorium in the borough.
claims.verbatim: Alexis Howell, who is running for the open Assembly seat D, agreed with the idea of a moratorium in the borough.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Byline Alex Bengel, published September 29th at 4:38 PM AKDT even though the URL path says 09/30. That's one day before the window, so label it as the pre-election record or background. Candidate statements are on the record, so a secondary source is acceptable.

claims.claim: Howell said the borough's grid is struggling and that she would "hate to see us dump a data center on top of that."
claims.verbatim: I would hate to see us dump a data center on top of that.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Confirmed present on two fetches. The grid fragment on the page reads 'the borough's grid is currently struggling', with a curly apostrophe normalized to straight. Background date as in C39.

claims.claim: Ramirez said he couldn't take a side on data centers without more study, saying "I can't really say 'yay' or 'nay' because I think there need to be more studies done."
claims.verbatim: I can't really say 'yay' or 'nay' because I think there need to be more studies done.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Curly quotes and apostrophes on the page are normalized to straight, and the wording is identical. The article also says he wants 'a study on these centers' environmental impact before they are built'. It doesn't name his seat but calls him Howell's opponent. KUAC on August 2nd confirms Ramirez is running for Seat D.

claims.claim: LaJiness, seeking reelection to Seat E, said "I don't think that data centers are good for any community, to be honest with you."
claims.verbatim: I don't think that data centers are good for any community, to be honest with you.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Curly apostrophe normalized. The article introduces him as 'Nick LaJiness, running for reelection to seat E, didn't mince words on his opinion on data centers'. It also misspells his name 'LaJinness' once. Use the ballot spelling, LaJiness.

claims.claim: Shupe described herself as between voters worried about data centers and those who don't want to dismiss them.
claims.verbatim: I'm somewhere in between the 'I'm worried about what it might bring' and 'I don't want to discount it' groups.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Curly quotes normalized. She's identified as 'Shelly Shupe, meanwhile, who is running for the same seat' (Seat E). KUAC on August 2nd says she serves on the borough commission for the Moose Creek Service Area.

claims.claim: Crass, running to keep Seat H, defended his vote for the data center moratorium.
claims.verbatim: Scott Crass, who is running to retain seat H on the Assembly, defended his vote in favor of the moratorium.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: The article also says Crass considered that 'a data center which supplied its own power might be a different conversation'. Crass was among the 6 in the 6-1 vote (C49). The article doesn't name the lone no vote.

claims.claim: Crass said "Energy costs in our community have skyrocketed."
claims.verbatim: Energy costs in our community have skyrocketed.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Exact match confirmed. Background date.

claims.claim: Leaders said he supports a temporary moratorium while data is collected and is open to data centers that benefit the community.
claims.verbatim: he supports a temporary moratorium while data is collected
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: His quote fragment on the page reads 'and we need to see if that benefit outweighs the cost', about infrastructure, grid and water impacts. He's identified as 'Joshua Leaders, who hopes to unseat Crass from seat H'. The point to carry is that all six candidates were short of an outright yes on data centers, while their degree of caution differed.

claims.claim: On August 27th the Assembly voted 6-1 to adopt 2027 legislative priorities that include a moratorium on commercial data centers.
claims.verbatim: voted 6-1 in favor of adopting a set of legislative priorities for 2027
claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)
claims.notes: Background. KUAC, August 31st, says only that the Assembly approved the priorities and doesn't give the count. The resolution text (C50) shows August 27th as the introduction date. The 6-1 count is single-sourced to Alaska's News Source; no roll call was reachable. Hedge with 'according to Alaska's News Source'. The no vote isn't named.

claims.claim: Resolution 2026-25, identifying and supporting legislative priorities, was introduced August 27th by the Assembly's Committee of the Whole.
claims.verbatim: A RESOLUTION IDENTIFYING AND SUPPORTING LEGISLATIVE PRIORITIES
claims.source_outlet: Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly, CivicClerk meeting file
claims.notes: Background, primary. The page also shows 'Resolution No. 2026 - 25' (punctuation normalized), 'Introduced: August 27, 2026' and 'Committee of the Whole'. Only the first 100,000 of about 1.8M characters were read, and the data center text was in that part.

claims.claim: Resolution 2026-25 supports a moratorium on the permitting, leasing or construction of new commercial data centers on state-owned or municipal lands in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: The FNSB supports a moratorium on the permitting, leasing, or construction of new commercial data centers on state-owned or municipal lands in Alaska
claims.source_outlet: Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly, CivicClerk meeting file
claims.notes: The heading is 'Moratorium on Data Center Development in Alaska'. The text doesn't say 'AI'. KUAC frames it as an AI data center moratorium. Federal and military land isn't in the text, though KUAC reports Crass said it was meant to cover federal lands too ('it was intended to include federal lands, as well'). Hedge that point as Crass's reported intent.

claims.claim: The moratorium would last until the state and local governments adopt standards addressing six named impacts, electrical demand, water consumption and shortages, environmental impacts, noise, air quality, and land use pollution.
claims.verbatim: have developed and adopted standards addressing electrical demand, water consumption and shortages, environmental impacts, noise, air quality, and land use pollution,
claims.source_outlet: Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly, CivicClerk meeting file
claims.notes: The text continues 'and other public interest considerations associated with data center development.' The preceding clause is 'until the State of Alaska and local governments'. The verbatim joins two line-broken fragments returned by WebFetch. 'Six' is our count of the listed items.

claims.claim: The data center moratorium was the only item to appear on both the state and federal parts of the Assembly's 2027 priorities list.
claims.verbatim: But only one item appears as a priority in both state and federal parts of the list
claims.source_outlet: KUAC
claims.notes: Background (August 31st, by Patrick Gilchrist). Primary corroboration: the resolution (C51) shows the same heading and text under both the state and the Federal Legislative Priorities. KUAC also reports 'a successful amendment replicated it as a federal priority, too'.

claims.claim: The Assembly's 2027 list totals 25 priorities split between the state and federal levels.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly's list is split between the state and federal levels, totaling 25 priorities.
claims.source_outlet: KUAC
claims.notes: Background. Curly apostrophe normalized. Not counted against the resolution itself, which wasn't read in full. KUAC also reports that Assemblymember Garret Armstrong proposed the moratorium as a state priority at an August 6th work session.

claims.claim: The Pentagon wants to build up to a dozen military data centers near Anchorage, Healy and Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: The Pentagon wants to build up to a dozen new military data centers near Anchorage, Healy and Fairbanks.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Public Media and KUAC
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (September 15th, by Shelby Herbert, KUAC). The brief said 'Air Force', but the page attributes the plan to the Pentagon, so the claim says Pentagon. Alaska's News Source, September 29th, separately says the Defense Department announced potential AI data centers near three Alaska installations 'including Eielson Air Force Base'. The article notes the Assembly can't direct the Pentagon on military land.

claims.claim: A newly installed camera at the South Anchorage Lowe's was cut down at about 11:28 p.m. on October 4th, according to a report Lowe's filed.

The store is on Old Seward Highway. The page says 'APD confirmed Lowe's filed a report stating' that it happened. KTOO, October 7th, independently reports, citing ADN, that at least one camera at an Anchorage Lowe's was cut down. Attribute the timing to the Lowe's report.

claims.claim: Anchorage police confirmed the downed device was a Flock camera and not a municipal streetlight.

claims.source_outlet: Alaska's News Source (KTUU)

The page also says Flock 'initially told Alaska's News Source on Monday it was not aware of any cameras in Alaska.' Smith also said private customers can't access law enforcement data; the page has that line in the uncontracted form, so it isn't quoted here because of the site contraction gate. Flock declined to name the customer. Don't name Lowe's as the customer, because Flock didn't.

claims.claim: APD's Real Time Crime Center page says the department doesn't use Flock cameras, and APD said it has no access to any video feed from the business.

KTOO, October 7th, independently says Anchorage police told ADN they don't have access to the data. Two claims joined, so split them if the deck uses either alone.

killed.claim: Koniag IT Systems' parent is Koniag Inc. of Kodiak.
killed.why: None of the fetched pages say it. The war.gov listing, ExecutiveBiz, koniag.com and koniag-gs.com all fail to name Koniag Inc. or a Kodiak headquarters as parent. koniag.com mentions Kodiak Island only as the Alutiiq homeland. Use C65 (Koniag Government Services subsidiary, an Alaska Native Corporation) instead.

killed.claim: The Air Force offered 4,700 acres for up to 12 AI data centers.
killed.why: The source attributes the plan to the Pentagon, not the Air Force, and doesn't name the bases. It's restated as C55 and C56 with Pentagon attribution.

killed.claim: APD says no report was filed on the downed Flock camera.
killed.why: It's superseded. The URL slug carries the old headline, but the current page says 'APD confirmed Lowe's filed a report'.

killed.claim: The South Anchorage Lowe's camera was Alaska's first Flock camera (as a flat fact).
killed.why: Alaska's News Source doesn't say 'first'. Flock said only that it began installing for one private Alaska customer the week before. It survives only in the hedged form, C73 (according to KTOO) plus C68.

killed.claim: Flock's private Alaska customer is Lowe's.
killed.why: Flock declined to share contract specifics. KTOO, citing ADN, says Lowe's stores installed cameras, but no source states Lowe's is the private customer Flock described.

killed.claim: The Assembly's moratorium resolution explicitly covers federal or military land.
killed.why: The resolution text names only state-owned or municipal lands. That Crass intended federal lands is his reported intent (KUAC), not the text. The Alaska Public Media report says the Assembly can't direct the Pentagon on military land.

killed.claim: Juneau's license plate camera data is kept for a stated period.
killed.why: KTOO doesn't give a retention period, and Barr said he doesn't know whether the data is stored with Genetec.
